summary:
Section 198 of Brunei's Syariah Penal Code creates the trans-specific offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa". Official guidance on the code states that it binds all persons in the country including tourists, and travel agents are briefed to that effect.

Human Rights Watch's #OUTLAWED survey places Brunei among at least two countries, with Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex. A comparable state-sharia offence operates in neighbouring Malaysia. The same survey records that at least 67 countries criminalise same-sex relations and at least nine criminalise gender expression.

The US State Department's 2017 report on human rights practices in Brunei describes the provision as banning men from dressing as women and women from dressing as men "without reasonable excuse", with no known convictions recorded in 2017. Morality provisions covering cross-dressing were among those enforced under the code at that time, while the sharia implementing regulations had not been issued. The same report records LGBTI-reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services.

There is one documented prosecution for cross-dressing: on 11 March 2015 a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for the offence. No later conviction has been sourced.

Stage 3 of the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 took effect on 3 April 2019. It prescribes death by stoning for anal sex and adultery, amputation for theft, and 40 strokes of the cane for sex between women. Sex between men was already a criminal offence under the prior law carrying up to 10 years' imprisonment. The code applies in the main to Muslims, who make up about two-thirds of the population.

Where the higher evidentiary standards of the sharia code are not met, fallback penalties remain available: sex between men carries up to seven years' imprisonment and 30 strokes of whipping, and for unmarried men one year in prison or 100 lashes; sex between women is punishable by any two of 40 lashes, up to 10 years' imprisonment, and a fine of up to B$40,000.

Brunei has carried out no execution since 1957. The sultan stated in April 2019 that the capital-punishment moratorium covers the new sharia penal code, and the moratorium remained intact as at a September 2026 freshness check.

Brunei does not permit a person to change their name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not allowed. A visitor's passport or other identity documents therefore cannot be brought into alignment with presentation.

LGBTI individuals have reported intimidation by police, including threats to make their sexuality public, interference with the ability to obtain a government job, and obstruction of graduation from government academic institutions. Members of the community also reported government monitoring of their activities and communications, and events on LGBTI topics have been subject to restrictions on assembly, with permits reportedly refused.

The code drew formal condemnation: Human Rights Watch called it "barbaric", the UN High Commissioner urged Brunei to halt it, and the United Nations and foreign governments condemned it as it took effect. OutRight Action International has described Brunei as the country with the most worrisome state of rights for LGBT people in Southeast Asia. Anyone convicted of "tarnishing the image of Islam" may be heavily punished, and first-person reporting from April 2019 describes a climate of fear with no assurance of enforcement against foreigners.
tangentialFactors:
Bruneian society tends to associate homosexuality with "effeminate men", which raises the visibility risk for gender-nonconforming visitors even where the trans-specific offence is not charged. Media outlets inside the country described the sharia provisions as "medieval" and "uncivilized" when stage 3 came into force.

The trans-specific offence is unusual in international terms. Among at least 67 jurisdictions criminalising same-sex relations, only at least nine criminalise gender expression as such, and Brunei's express "posing as" wording is shared with Oman alone while Malaysia reaches a similar result through state sharia provisions.

Reporting from April 2019 by France24 and TIME documents fear in the LGBTI community as the stoning penalties took effect, with sources speaking anonymously; TIME also noted no assurance of enforcement against foreigners. The population affected is small, roughly 420,000 to 450,000 depending on the source, and about two-thirds Muslim.

The UN and several foreign governments condemned the code at the time of its final stage, and corporate and diplomatic pressure was widely reported in that period; the practical effect of that pressure on enforcement is not documented in the sources held here.
localsOnly:
The Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 applies in the main to Muslims, who constitute about two-thirds of the population, but official guidance circulated to travel agents states that the code's provisions, including the cross-dressing offence, bind all persons in the country.

Residents cannot change name or gender markers on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not permitted, so identity paperwork remains inconsistent with presentation for the duration of a person's life in Brunei.

Government employment and graduation are documented pressure points: LGBTI residents reported police threats to disclose their sexuality, interference with government job applications, and obstruction of graduation from government academic institutions. Events on LGBTI topics have been refused assembly permits, and community members reported monitoring of their activities and communications.

Discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services was reported to the US State Department in 2017. Morality provisions covering cross-dressing, alcohol, eating during Ramadan and religious propagation were being enforced at that time, with the sharia implementing regulations still unissued.

Corporal punishment is prescribed under the code and remains the sentence of record where the higher evidentiary thresholds are not met: up to seven years and 30 strokes for sex between men, one year or 100 lashes for unmarried men, and any two of 40 lashes, 10 years' imprisonment and a B$40,000 fine for sex between women. No execution has been carried out since 1957, and the moratorium declared in 2019 covers the sharia penalties.
outOfScopeNotes:
The primary statutory text could not be verified directly: the hosted copy of Brunei's Penal Code including the Syariah Penal Code provisions returned HTTP 403 at research time, as did an SSRN paper on the sharia penal code. Section 198's wording here rests on secondary description rather than the enacted text.

Unresolved: whether the sharia implementing regulations, still unissued as at the 2017 US State Department report, have since been promulgated. The sources held do not say.

Unresolved: whether Section 198 has been charged after the 11 March 2015 fine, and whether the offence has been applied to foreign visitors. Reporting from April 2019 states there was no assurance of enforcement against foreigners, which is not the same as an exemption.

Unresolved: the current population figure. Sources give about 420,000 and about 450,000 for the same period.

The France24 and TIME pieces of April 2019 are first-person and community reporting; they establish fear and perceived risk but do not document a specific prosecution or acquittal.
